newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK government ready to swing into action.
newsitem.headline: New HK government ready to swing into action.

text.p: Hong Kong's new post-colonial government launched into its first full week of business on Monday, gearing up for a key cabinet meeting and a legislative session that were to set the tone for the future.
But, like a voice from the grave, last British governor Chris Patten leaped back into Hong Kong politics from afar, charging that Britain had delayed democracy here in order to appease China.
Tung Chee-hwa, chosen by a Beijing-controlled committee to lead the new Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, was set to convene his Executive Council on Tuesday, officials said.
High on the agenda for Exco, as the advisory group is familiarly known, was a crisis over illegal immigration involving thousands of children from mainland China.
It was also expected to discuss what electoral system should replace the one put in place by the colonial government and scrapped by Beijing when it took back the territory on July 1.
On Wednesday, Tung was to pay his first visit to the People's Liberation Army's (PLA) on Stonecutters Island. The PLA has almost 5,000 troops in the region responsible for the defence of Hong Kong.

Under the agreement with Britain that led to last Tuesday's handover, China has promised Hong Kong's 6.4 million people they may keep their capitalistic way of life for half a century. The SAR's government is to enjoy broad autonomy with Beijing responsible only for defence and foreign affairs.
Exco is to set out the new government's priorities for bills to be presented to the Provisional Legislature, officials said.

The highly controversial, unelected legislature -- which China set up to replace the assembly elected under British auspices in 1995 -- is to hold its first regular post-handover session on Wednesday.
"We have to wait for tomorrow's Exco meeting to see whether the government will table any bills (at the legislature)," an official at the legislature's secretariat said.

Tung and his 15 close advisers are widely expected to tackle the crisis over a tide of illegal immigration from mainland China, primarily children smuggled into Hong Kong to join parents who are already residents.

Hundreds of families have taken their children to Hong Kong's immigration office in the past few days to register and apply for residency rights, believing the new government will not send them back to the mainland.

Most of the "child illegals" have Hong Kong fathers and, under the territory's post-handover constitution, have the theoretical right to live here. The problem is that many relatives have jumped the gun, sneaking the children in without waiting to obtain formal clearance from the authorities.
It is estimated that 60,000 children from "split families" are waiting to settle in Hong Kong.

Exco's discussions on a proposed new electoral system are important because, until rules can be drawn up and new legislative elections held, Tung will have to field accusations that the unelected interim chamber is unconstitutional.

Tung has promised that the first post-handover election will be held in the second quarter of 1998. He is now pondering which system should be used, how many geographical seats to establish and whether to use proportional representation.

Patten's charges, contained in a book to be published this week, said Britain twisted Hong Kong people's views on a plan for greater democracy in 1988 in a bow to Chinese demand for a delay in direct elections.

"If I were a citizen of Hong Kong, I would regard it as very bad that I hadn't been kept in the know and that my views had been treated in this way," Patten was quoted as saying by Jonathan Dimbleby, author of "The Last Governor".
Martin Lee, Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp leader who was ousted from the legislature after last week's handover, seized upon Patten's allegations and demanded a public inquiry.
"I think the documents should be certainly given to the Foreign Affairs Committee," Lee told reporters.
